section_summary: This section spans 1932–1939 and documents Japanese intelligence, espionage, influence operations, and propaganda in China, including approaches to journalists and foreign technical experts. It contains diplomatic reporting on Japanese-controlled propaganda in Wuhan and Canton, with extensive translations of anti-British articles advocating Sino-Japanese cooperation and a Japanese-sponsored “New Order” in East Asia. Other records concern suspected military uses of imported timber, espionage arrests, propaganda about American military assistance to China, and cross-references to related reports and Japanese war literature.

subfiles.title: Document file note: pressure on E. S. Durassoff
subfiles.about: The note cross-references a report about Soviet and Japanese secret-police pressure on an American consular clerk in Harbin.
subfiles.summary: File note: E. S. Durassoff, a Harbin consulate general clerk, was pressured by Soviet and Japanese secret authorities (125.4613/273).

subfiles.title: Telegram concerning Japanese purchases of Port Orford cedar
subfiles.about: Prince warns that large Japanese purchases of Port Orford cedar might conceal preparations for mines or another destructive military purpose.
subfiles.summary: O. A. Prince urges consideration of heavy Japanese purchases of Port Orford cedar logs over three years, reportedly submerged in Shanghai harbor, possibly to camouflage mine-laying or another destructive aim.

subfiles.title: Document file note: Japanese liaison officer’s approach to a correspondent
subfiles.about: The note reports an alleged Japanese financial approach to an American newspaper correspondent and a possible similar approach to a League of Nations committee.
subfiles.summary: A Japanese liaison officer allegedly offered an American Shanghai correspondent money to portray events 'as they are', and was expected to approach a League committee similarly.

subfiles.title: Transmittal of Tientsin despatch no. 116
subfiles.from: F. P. Lockhart, American Consul General, Tientsin
subfiles.about: Lockhart forwards copies of his despatch no. 116 to the Legation at Beijing.
subfiles.summary: Lockhart transmits Tientsin Despatch No. 116 on the alleged capture of Japanese newspapermen and John Meijbroek's activities.

subfiles.title: Alleged Capture of Japanese Newspaper Men
subfiles.from: F. P. Lockhart, American Consul General, Tientsin
subfiles.to: Nelson T. Johnson, American Minister, Peiping
subfiles.about: Lockhart reports an alleged secret mission by John N. Meijbroek to secure the release of four Japanese newspaper men held near Shanhaiguan.
subfiles.summary: Winans's letter: Meijbroek tried to obtain help releasing four Japanese newspapermen reportedly captured outside the Great Wall; Lockhart finds it extraordinary the capture was unreported.

subfiles.title: Letter reporting Meijbroek’s mission
subfiles.about: Winans reports that John N. Meijbroek sought assistance in arranging the release of Japanese newspaper men.
subfiles.summary: Winans says Meijbroek tried to free Japanese newspapermen reportedly held at Luanzhou, money first, with Japanese military action possible; mentions his Tangshan movements.

subfiles.title: Document file note: Economic Intelligence Commission
subfiles.about: The note describes the South Manchuria Railway Company’s formation of an Economic Intelligence Commission associated with the Japanese Army.
subfiles.summary: File note: an Economic Intelligence Commission was reportedly organized to consolidate Japanese Army gains in Manchuria (895.77/2848).

subfiles.title: Document file note: Japanese Information Bureau propaganda
subfiles.about: The note identifies a telegram concerning English-language propaganda issued by the Japanese Information Bureau at Tianjin.
subfiles.summary: File note: the Japanese Information Bureau was disseminating English-language news propaganda, with examples in telegram no. 1321.

subfiles.title: Telegram no. 1321: examples of Japanese news propaganda
subfiles.from: American Legation, Peiping, for the Minister by Engert
subfiles.about: The telegram reproduces Japanese propaganda alleging American arms sales and expanding American military influence in China.
subfiles.summary: The first item claims that Zhang Xueliang and Chu Ching Lang purchased American aircraft, antiaircraft guns, machine guns, and trench mortars. The second alleges that Chinese authorities planned to replace German specialists with American instructors in aviation, chemical warfare, poison gas, and smoke-screen training.

subfiles.title: Document file note: Japanese aspersions on foreign intentions
subfiles.about: The note references a despatch reporting Japanese efforts to discredit other nations’ intentions toward China.
subfiles.summary: File note: Japanese news agencies broadened propaganda beyond Manchuria to cast doubt on other powers' motives toward China.

subfiles.title: Extract from despatch no. 221 on Japanese news propaganda
subfiles.about: The extract lists Japanese allegations that an American wheat loan concealed munitions purchases and that foreign powers were expanding their spheres of influence in China.
subfiles.summary: Despatch No. 221 extract: Japanese agencies claimed only part of the American wheat loan would buy wheat, the rest munitions, and accused powers of enlarging spheres of influence, including through aviation aid.

subfiles.title: Document file note: Chengchow espionage case
subfiles.about: The note identifies a report about three Japanese and one Chinese accused of espionage and fomenting disturbances in Henan.
subfiles.summary: File note: the Chengchow case involved four alleged agents arrested for espionage for Japan and encouraging unrest in Henan.

subfiles.title: Report extract: Chengchow espionage case
subfiles.about: The extract reports the arrest of three Japanese and one Chinese at Zhengzhou on espionage charges.
subfiles.summary: Four men arrested January 5 with documents seized; the Japanese suspects went to the Japanese consul, while Chinese officials alleged spying and fomenting disturbances in Henan.

subfiles.title: Despatch no. 490: Enquiry for address of Mr. Leeland Andrus
subfiles.from: Willys R. Peck, for the Ambassador, Nanking
subfiles.about: The Embassy reports its guarded handling of F. W. Poate Jr.’s request for Leeland Andrus’s address.
subfiles.summary: The despatch encloses Poate’s request, the Embassy’s reply, and a memorandum explaining the reply. Although officials considered Andrus’s suspicions somewhat far-fetched, they honored his request not to disclose his location and reported the matter as potentially significant.

subfiles.title: Letter seeking Leeland Andrus’s address
subfiles.about: Poate asks American officials to locate Leeland Andrus on behalf of a purported sister in Honolulu.
subfiles.summary: Poate seeks the address of Leeland Andrus, a wireless expert at Nanjing's Central Aviation School, for Mrs. McDonough of Honolulu; letters returned as unknown.

subfiles.title: Embassy reply to F. W. Poate Jr.
subfiles.from: J. Hall Paxton, for the Ambassador
subfiles.about: The Embassy tells Poate that Andrus’s wife denied he had a sister of the stated name in Honolulu.
subfiles.summary: Embassy tells Poate, without revealing Andrus's location, that Mrs. Andrus says her husband has no sister of that name in Honolulu.

subfiles.title: Memorandum of conversation: whereabouts of Leeland Andrus
subfiles.about: Andrus explains why he believes Poate’s inquiry originated with Japanese agents seeking contact with or influence over him.
subfiles.summary: Andrus denies a sister named McDonough, calls Poate a suspicious British acquaintance, says his letters were repeatedly opened, and that Chinese intelligence tied such inquiries to Japanese agencies; requests a noncommittal reply.

subfiles.title: Despatch no. 504: follow-up on the Andrus inquiry
subfiles.from: Willys R. Peck, for the Ambassador, Nanking
subfiles.about: The Embassy forwards Poate’s response to its earlier handling of his request for Andrus’s address.
subfiles.summary: Despatch No. 504 follows up the Andrus inquiry, enclosing Poate's reply of June 7 without disclosing Andrus's location.

subfiles.title: Poate’s acknowledgment of the Embassy reply
subfiles.about: Poate accepts that Andrus may have no sister in Honolulu and says he will forward the Embassy’s reply without comment.
subfiles.summary: Poate acknowledges the Embassy's June 5 letter, calls the explanation possible, apologizes and thanks it.

subfiles.title: Document file note: Japanese air-dropped posters over Wuhan
subfiles.about: The note cross-references translations of posters dropped by Japanese aircraft during an air raid on Wuhan.
subfiles.summary: File note: Japanese aircraft allegedly dropped propaganda posters over Wuhan, with translations enclosed.

subfiles.title: Despatch: Anti-foreign Propaganda
subfiles.from: R. Y. Jarvis, American Consul, Hankow
subfiles.about: Jarvis forwards Japanese-sponsored Wuhan propaganda attacking Western powers, particularly Britain.
subfiles.summary: Jarvis encloses a Wuhan Peace Maintenance Society circular and translated Wuhan Pao articles defending Japan's invasion, attacking Chiang and communism, and reviving charges of white imperialism; little Chinese response.

subfiles.title: Original Wuhan Peace Maintenance Society circular
subfiles.from: Bureau of Social Affairs, Wuhan Peace Maintenance Society
subfiles.about: This is the Chinese original of a Japanese-sponsored circular explaining the occupation and urging peace and cooperation with Japan.
subfiles.summary: Original Chinese Wuhan Peace Maintenance Society circular of March 28, with 'What the People of Wuhan Should Hereafter Know'; OCR lacks the text.

subfiles.title: What the People of Wuhan Should Hereafter Know
subfiles.from: Bureau of Social Affairs, Wuhan Peace Maintenance Society
subfiles.about: The circular condemns Chiang Kai-shek, justifies Japan’s invasion, promotes Sino-Japanese cooperation, and appeals for acceptance of the occupation order.
subfiles.summary: Circular presents Chiang's Russian alliance and resistance as disastrous, accuses Western powers of exploiting China, casts Japan's expedition as saving both nations, and urges support for Wang Jingwei and Konoe's New Order.

subfiles.title: Construction of a New China and Anti-British Movement
subfiles.about: The article depicts British financial support for Chiang Kai-shek as the principal obstruction to peace and calls for action against Britain.
subfiles.summary: Article claims Chiang's resistance would collapse without British loans, calls Britain the Chinese people's enemy and endorses demands to recover concessions and deport British residents.

subfiles.title: Reminiscences on the Shameen Tragedy
subfiles.about: The article recounts the 1925 Shamian and Shaji violence as historical justification for renewed anti-British agitation.
subfiles.summary: Article recalls the Shameen shooting after the May Thirtieth incident, accusing British forces of machine-gunning demonstrators near Shamian's West Bridge and stressing deaths and boycott, in inflammatory language.

subfiles.title: Historical Facts of British Aggression in China, first installment
subfiles.doc_type: translated newspaper report of a broadcast
subfiles.from: General Headquarters of the Ta Ming Hui, reprinted by Wuhan Pao
subfiles.about: The broadcast presents a polemical history of British expansion in China from the Opium War through intervention in Tibet.
subfiles.summary: Broadcast report, first installment: Lin Zexu's destruction of opium, Opium War treaties, Burma, Boxer settlement, leases, Lhasa expedition and British separatism in Tibet, as British aggression, linked to cooperation with Chiang.

subfiles.title: Historical Facts of British Aggression in China, second installment
subfiles.about: The article extends its account of alleged British aggression from the early Republic through the contemporary Sino-Japanese War.
subfiles.summary: Second installment: Britain used Yuan Shikai and militarists, cites May Thirtieth and later shootings, and says British loans let Chiang continue the war.

subfiles.title: Anti-British Movement
subfiles.about: The editorial calls for a nationwide anti-British movement in support of the Japanese-sponsored political order.
subfiles.summary: Editorial welcomes anti-British organizations across several provinces, invokes the Opium War and May Thirtieth, urges joining anti-colonial movements in Burma and India and overthrowing Chiang and British interests.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference: anti-foreign propaganda through Japanese puppets
subfiles.about: The sheet points to a report on anti-foreign propaganda disseminated through puppet organizations in Japanese-occupied China.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference to Jinan Despatch No. 69 (793.94/15064): anti-foreign propaganda through Japanese puppets.

subfiles.title: Department memorandum on Japanese propaganda at Canton
subfiles.from: Division of Far Eastern Affairs, Department of State
subfiles.about: The memorandum summarizes a Canton report describing the shift of Japanese propaganda toward anti-British themes during the Anglo-Japanese crisis.
subfiles.summary: Memo: Guangzhou propaganda, earlier aimed at Chiang and communism, turned anti-British during the Anglo-Japanese crisis, with hints the Army might act against Hong Kong.

subfiles.title: Covering despatch: Japanese Propaganda in Canton
subfiles.from: M. S. Myers, American Consul General, Canton
subfiles.about: Myers forwards a copy of his despatch no. 26 to the Embassy at Beijing concerning Japanese propaganda in Guangzhou.
subfiles.summary: Covering despatch transmitting Despatch No. 26 on Japanese propaganda in occupied Guangzhou, dated July 19, 1939.

subfiles.title: Despatch no. 26: Japanese Propaganda in Canton
subfiles.from: M. S. Myers, American Consul General, Canton
subfiles.to: Nelson Trusler Johnson, American Ambassador, Peiping
subfiles.about: Myers reports the media, themes, and increasing anti-British emphasis of Japanese propaganda in occupied Guangzhou.
subfiles.summary: Despatch No. 26: since October 1938 Japanese posters, newspapers and radio attacked Chiang and communism; during the Tianjin crisis they invoked British aggression; a Japanese Army statement voiced concern about Hong Kong.

subfiles.title: Statement of the Japanese Army Authorities in Canton
subfiles.from: Japanese Army authorities in Canton, published by the Canton Daily Sun
subfiles.about: The statement supports Japanese demands in the Tianjin crisis and warns Britain to abandon its pro-Chiang and allegedly anti-Japanese policies.
subfiles.summary: Garbled clipping: the Japanese South China forces say they will ensure Britain changes course, accusing it of obstructing operations, backing Chiang and disturbing the new order.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference: English translations of Japanese war novels
subfiles.about: The sheet points to a despatch enclosing English translations of the Japanese war novels Mud and Soldiers and Barley and Soldiers.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference: English translations of Japanese war novels by K. Bush and L. W. Bush, filed with Despatch No. 4054 (793.94/15318).
